analysis.one_liner: Lets US pharmacies and wholesalers reimport American-made prescription drugs sold cheaper abroad.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Energy and Commerce subcommittee until the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2000, Congress created a program letting pharmacies and wholesalers bring US-made prescription drugs back from countries where they sell for less, but the program was written with requirements that made it nearly impossible to use. This bill would have rewritten those rules: it would ease the testing and labeling requirements, bar drug makers from using contracts or supply limits to block reimported drugs, and forbid makers from discriminating against US pharmacies, wholesalers, or consumers. It also ordered a government study of how the imports worked and authorized funding to run the program. The bill was introduced in February 2001, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its Health Subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who fill prescriptions, especially seniors and people paying US retail prices that are far higher than what the same drugs cost in Canada and Europe, plus pharmacists and wholesalers who could import lower-priced drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Prescription drug buyers and US pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: The bill would ease the testing requirements for reimported drugs, allowing importers to use the labeling already approved for the product in the US, and let the Health Secretary waive testing where agreements ensure products are not adulterated [S3].

It would prohibit drug manufacturers from entering contracts or agreements that prevent the sale or distribution of reimported drugs, and from discriminating against US pharmacists, wholesalers, or consumers in how drugs are sold [S3].

It would define discrimination to include contract terms or supply limits that give US buyers less favorable access than foreign purchasers get, closing a loophole manufacturers could use to keep cheap drugs out of American hands [S3].

It would order the Comptroller General to study compliance with the import program and any counterfeit or adulterated shipments, and authorize funding so the program could actually be carried out [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would lose the ability to charge US patients far more than they charge the same drugs to foreign buyers.

drawbacks.text: Safety was the central objection: a 2000 law required the Health Secretary to certify that reimportation posed no added risk, and the agency's position was that it could not guarantee the safety of the drug supply once products moved through foreign channels; testing of imported products imposes real costs and trade-secret questions, which the bill partially addresses but does not eliminate [S3].

The bill's own text acknowledges the risk by requiring the Comptroller General to count any shipments found counterfeit, misbranded, or adulterated and to evaluate effects on trade and patent rights, an admission that imported products could include fakes and that patent enforcement would be complicated [S3].

Reimportation only addresses prices of US-manufactured drugs sold abroad; it does nothing for generic competition or for drugs priced similarly everywhere, and manufacturers could shift pricing or supply abroad in response, so the savings for consumers might be smaller than hoped [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers facing some of the highest prescription drug prices in the world, the potential savings from buying the same US-made drugs at foreign prices are large, and the bill was written to make the existing reimportation program workable rather than to open an unregulated channel. The honest cost is safety risk and enforcement complexity: imported products are harder to authenticate, and the bill trades a stricter regime for testing, waiver, and nondiscrimination rules that try to manage that risk. The trade-off is real but the bill took it seriously; the bigger question is whether Congress ever gave it a hearing, and it did not.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in March 2001, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Bernard Sanders introduced the bill on February 14, 2001, amending the drug reimportation program created the previous year to make it usable by pharmacists and wholesalers [S1].
Forty House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans appear among the cosponsors on record [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S1].
On March 14, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where the action history ends; no further action was taken before the 107th Congress ended in January 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept their US price structure intact, since a reimportation channel that would have let American pharmacies buy the same drugs at foreign prices was never allowed to function.

for.name: Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 40 Democratic cosponsors for it.

for.name: 40 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the reimportation bill; the bill's original cosponsors included Reps. Deutsch, Brown of Ohio, Bonior, Kaptur, DeLauro, Conyers, and Nadler.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never reported it out; it was sent to the Health Subcommittee on March 14, 2001, and no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, controlled the committee calendar while the bill sat without a hearing or markup until the Congress ended; he later left Congress to become president of the pharmaceutical industry's main lobbying group.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and brand-name drug makers
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained public campaign against drug reimportation, arguing it endangered the drug supply and undermined patient safety.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors in the record were the Independent lead sponsor plus 40 House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill died in a Republican-controlled committee without a vote [S4].

industries.note: Reimportation would have let US pharmacies and wholesalers buy American-made drugs at the lower prices charged abroad, undercutting the price discrimination that lets manufacturers charge US patients the most in the world. The bill also bans contracts and supply limits designed to block that channel.

The bill's whole design targets 'importation by pharmacists and wholesalers,' easing their testing and labeling burdens and protecting them from manufacturer discrimination, so they could pass lower prices to customers.
